title: Search, embeddings and RAG
summary: Baseline first: BM25 and retrieval metrics plus a frozen test harness come before any embedding trick. Then provenance-first ingestion, chunking (incl. contextual retrieval), embedding selection/efficiency, ANN indexes, permission-aware vector DBs, hybrid + rerank, query transformations, grounded answering with citations/abstention, and calibrated end-to-end RAG evaluation. Spine: LLM Zoomcamp 2026 + IR book + vendor-neutral docs; LangChain RAG From Scratch only for query-transformation concepts.

units.title: Information retrieval basics, BM25 and ranking metrics
outcomes: You can implement BM25 from scratch and explain k1 (term-frequency saturation) and b (length normalization).
You can implement recall@k, MRR and nDCG@10 and unit-test them on toy rankings.
You can say when lexical search beats dense retrieval (IDs, codes, rare terms).

practice.title: BM25 + metrics from scratch
practice.brief: Implement BM25 (k1, b) yourself and compare its rankings with rank_bm25 on one corpus (e.g. FBR tax FAQs or your university handbook). Implement recall@k, MRR and nDCG@10 and unit-test each on hand-made toy rankings with known answers. Sweep b ∈ {0, 0.5, 0.75, 1} and report nDCG@10.
practice.done_when: pytest passes for metric unit tests; your BM25 top-10 matches rank_bm25 on ≥95% of queries; a b-sweep table.

quiz.prompt: In BM25, parameter b controls:
quiz.explain: b=0 disables length normalization; b=1 fully normalizes by document length (k1 controls saturation).

quiz.prompt: MRR rewards:
options: The rank of the first relevant result
quiz.explain: Reciprocal rank = 1/rank of the first hit, averaged over queries.

quiz.prompt: nDCG handles graded relevance by:
options: Discounting gains logarithmically by rank and normalizing by the ideal ranking
quiz.explain: DCG/IDCG puts the score in [0,1] and rewards highly relevant items near the top.

quiz.prompt: Why can BM25 beat dense retrieval on part numbers or legal section IDs?
rubric: Exact-token matching: IDs like 'Section 114(2)' are rare terms with high IDF
Dense embeddings blur exact strings into semantic neighbours and may not distinguish 114 vs 141
Conclusion: keep BM25 as a baseline/hybrid component

You can write one evaluate(retriever) → metrics.json harness that every later unit calls.
You can run component ablations that change one thing at a time.

practice.title: The harness every later unit uses
practice.brief: Create 60 questions with gold passage IDs (40 hand-written, 20 LLM-generated then human-filtered), plus 15 unanswerable and 10 permission-restricted questions (tagged with the user role allowed to see the answer). Write evaluate(retriever) → metrics.json (recall@k, MRR, nDCG@10, abstention, latency) and freeze a test split.
practice.done_when: metrics.json produced for the U01 BM25 baseline; test-set file with tags; split frozen with a recorded hash.

quiz.prompt: Unanswerable questions in a RAG test set measure:
quiz.explain: A good system says 'not found' instead of answering from irrelevant chunks.

quiz.prompt: LLM-generated questions should be filtered because they often:
options: Copy wording from the passage, inflating lexical-match scores
quiz.explain: Real users paraphrase; generated questions leak passage words.

quiz.prompt: A component ablation changes:
options: One component at a time with everything else fixed
quiz.explain: Otherwise you cannot attribute the metric change.

quiz.prompt: How many test questions do you need before you trust a 3-point recall@5 difference? Justify roughly.
rubric: Uses a binomial/bootstrap argument: SE ≈ sqrt(p(1−p)/n); at p≈0.7, ±3 points at 95% needs roughly n≈900 for unpaired
Notes paired comparisons on the same questions need fewer (variance of differences)
Concludes small sets only detect large differences

You can re-ingest incrementally so only changed documents are processed.

practice.title: Provenance-first ingestion
practice.brief: Ingest 20 mixed docs (a 2-column PDF, a scanned Urdu/English notice, an HTML page, a table-heavy PDF) with Docling or MarkItDown plus PyMuPDF. Store doc_id, content hash, source URL/page, char offsets and an ACL tag. Write an extraction-quality check (sampled visual diff + table-cell accuracy on 3 tables). Re-run and prove only changed files re-ingest.
practice.done_when: A store with all metadata fields populated, a quality report (cell accuracy on 3 tables), and a second run log showing 0 re-ingests for unchanged files and 1 for an edited file.

quiz.prompt: A content hash per document enables:
options: Skipping unchanged documents during incremental ingest
quiz.explain: Compare hashes; only re-chunk/re-embed what changed, and delete what vanished.

quiz.prompt: The most damaging silent error in PDF ingestion is often:
options: Wrong reading order in multi-column layouts
quiz.explain: Interleaved columns produce fluent-looking nonsense that still gets embedded.

quiz.prompt: Storing an ACL tag on each chunk lets you:
options: Filter results by user permission at query time
quiz.explain: Authorization must be enforced in retrieval, before generation.

quiz.prompt: Why must provenance (doc, page, offsets) be captured at ingest time rather than reconstructed later?
rubric: Later transformations (cleaning, chunking, OCR) lose the mapping back to source positions
Citations and audits need exact spans; reconstruction by fuzzy search is unreliable
Version hashes tie a citation to the exact document version

practice.title: Chunker bake-off
practice.brief: On your U02 harness run 4 chunkers (fixed-512, recursive, heading-aware, parent-child) × 2 overlaps. Add contextual annotation to the best config. Report recall@5, index size, ingest cost, and pass a citation-offset round-trip test (chunk text == source[start:end]). Implement ±1 neighbour expansion and near-duplicate chunk removal.
practice.done_when: A results table (8 configs + contextual variant) with recall@5/size/cost; round-trip test passes on 100% of chunks; dedup removes measured duplicates.

quiz.prompt: Parent-child chunking indexes ___ and returns ___:
options: Small child chunks for precise matching, larger parent sections for context
quiz.explain: Small chunks embed sharply; the parent gives the LLM enough surrounding text.

quiz.prompt: Larger chunk overlap always:
options: Increases index size and duplicate hits — it must be measured
quiz.explain: Overlap helps boundary cases but costs storage and crowds top-k with duplicates.

quiz.prompt: Contextual retrieval prepends to each chunk:
options: A short generated description situating it within the document
quiz.explain: Anthropic reported fewer retrieval failures when chunks carry document context.

quiz.prompt: How does keeping character offsets let you show exact source spans in answers?
rubric: Each chunk stores (doc_id, version, start, end) into the normalized source
Citations map back to source[start:end] (and page/coordinates) for highlighting
Offsets survive re-chunking only if tied to a document version hash

practice.brief: Compare 3 embedding models (one multilingual) on your harness, including Urdu queries, with the correct query/passage prefixes. practice.done_when: A table: model × (full / truncated / int8 / binary) × recall@5 × memory per 1M; a short decision note naming the model you will use and why.

quiz.prompt: If embeddings are L2-normalized, cosine similarity equals:
quiz.explain: cos(a,b) = a·b/(|a||b|) and both norms are 1.

quiz.prompt: 'query: / passage:' prefixes required by some models address:
options: The query–document asymmetry the model was trained with
quiz.explain: Omitting them silently lowers recall for such models.

quiz.prompt: A top MTEB average does not guarantee the best model for you because:
options: Your domain, language and task may differ from the benchmark mix
quiz.explain: Always re-evaluate on your own test set (Urdu is barely represented).

quiz.prompt: When would you fine-tune an embedding model instead of switching models?
rubric: When your domain vocabulary/queries are off-distribution and several off-the-shelf models plateau on your harness
When you have (or can generate and filter) enough query–passage pairs
Mentions cost: re-embedding the corpus and maintaining the model

practice.title: ANN trade-off curves
practice.brief: On 200k–1M vectors (e.g. Simple-English Wikipedia embeddings), compare IndexFlatIP, HNSW (M and efSearch sweep), IVF (nlist/nprobe sweep) and IVF-PQ. Compute recall@10 against the exact results and plot recall vs p95 latency and vs memory.
practice.done_when: Two plots (recall vs p95 latency, recall vs memory) with ≥4 points per index type; a recommendation for your corpus size.

quiz.prompt: HNSW's efSearch primarily trades:
quiz.explain: Larger efSearch explores more of the graph: slower, more accurate.

quiz.prompt: Product quantization reduces:
options: Memory per vector by encoding subvectors with codebooks
quiz.explain: A 768-d float32 vector (3 KB) can become tens of bytes.

quiz.prompt: ANN index recall is measured against:
options: Exact nearest-neighbour results for the same vectors
quiz.explain: Index recall isolates the approximation error from embedding quality.

quiz.prompt: Why can a perfect ANN index still give bad RAG results?
rubric: ANN recall only measures agreement with exact search over the same embeddings
If embeddings/chunking are poor, the exact neighbours are themselves irrelevant
End-to-end retrieval metrics on labelled questions are still needed

practice.title: Permission-aware vector store
practice.brief: Load your corpus into Postgres+pgvector (Docker). Implement tenant- and ACL-filtered search. Show the filtered-ANN recall problem (selective filter + HNSW returns too few results) and fix it with one mitigation (iterative index scans, partial index, or pre-filter). Then re-embed to a new model with versioned tables/collections and an alias/view switch while queries keep running.
practice.done_when: A test proving a user never receives chunks outside their ACL; before/after result counts for the filtered-ANN fix; a log showing zero failed queries during the re-embed switch.

quiz.prompt: Applying a selective metadata filter after ANN retrieval can:
options: Return too few results because filtered-out items consumed the top-k
quiz.explain: Post-filtering 10 candidates with a 5%-selective filter leaves ~0.5 results.

quiz.prompt: Changing the embedding model usually requires:
options: Re-embedding the corpus, since vectors from different models are not comparable
quiz.explain: Different models produce different vector spaces.

quiz.prompt: A good reason to choose pgvector over a dedicated vector DB:
options: Transactional joins with existing relational data and one system to operate
quiz.explain: For small-to-medium corpora, operational simplicity often wins.

quiz.prompt: Where must authorization filtering happen so the LLM never sees forbidden text?
rubric: In the retrieval query itself (filter by ACL/tenant before results are returned)
Never rely on the LLM or a post-generation filter to hide text it already saw
ACLs stored on every chunk and kept in sync with the source system

quiz.prompt: RRF combines rankers using:
options: The reciprocal of each item's rank in each list
quiz.explain: score = Σ 1/(k + rank); it ignores incomparable raw scores.

quiz.prompt: Hybrid search helps most when queries mix:
quiz.explain: BM25 catches exact strings; dense catches meaning.

quiz.prompt: Score-based fusion needs care because:
options: BM25 and cosine scores have different scales and distributions
quiz.explain: Normalize (min-max, z-score, DBSF) or use rank-based fusion.

quiz.prompt: Show a query from your set where hybrid wins over both components, and explain why.
rubric: Quotes the actual query and the ranks from BM25, dense and hybrid
Explains which part of the query each retriever matched
Connects to the fusion formula (both lists had it moderately high)

practice.title: Rerank depth sweep + MMR
practice.brief: Add a cross-encoder reranker over the hybrid top-50 and sweep rerank depth (20/50/100). Report nDCG@10 gain vs added p95 latency. Implement MMR (λ sweep) and show it reduces near-duplicate chunks in the final context without hurting recall@5.
practice.done_when: A depth × (nDCG@10, p95 latency) table and an MMR λ table with duplicate rate and recall@5.

quiz.prompt: A cross-encoder is slower than a bi-encoder because it:
options: Must jointly encode every query–document pair at query time
quiz.explain: Bi-encoder document vectors are precomputed; cross-encoders cannot be.

quiz.prompt: MMR balances:
quiz.explain: Each pick maximizes λ·relevance − (1−λ)·max similarity to already-picked items.

quiz.prompt: Two-stage retrieval means:
options: Cheap high-recall candidate retrieval, then expensive precise reranking
quiz.explain: Stage 1 maximizes recall; stage 2 maximizes precision at the top.

quiz.prompt: When is a reranker not worth its latency?
rubric: When measured nDCG/answer-quality gain on your harness is negligible (first stage already precise)
When latency budget is tight (e.g. autocomplete) or traffic is very high
When the first stage misses the relevant docs (reranking cannot recover recall)

quiz.prompt: HyDE embeds:
options: A hypothetical answer document generated from the query
quiz.explain: Answer-shaped text sits closer to real answer passages in embedding space.

quiz.prompt: The main cost of multi-query retrieval is:
options: Extra LLM and search calls, plus duplicate results to fuse
quiz.explain: N rewrites ≈ N searches and an extra LLM call per query.

quiz.prompt: GraphRAG is most justified for:
options: Global, relationship or 'summarize the corpus' questions
quiz.explain: Its community summaries target sensemaking over a whole corpus; index cost is high.

quiz.prompt: Why must an agentic retrieval loop have a step budget and a stop criterion?
rubric: Without them the model can loop, rack up cost/latency, or drift off the question
Stop criterion: sufficient evidence found / confidence threshold / no new results
Budget makes worst-case cost and latency predictable and testable

practice.title: Grounded answer step
practice.brief: Build the answer step: numbered sources, span-level citations (doc_id + offsets) validated after generation, abstention ('not found in the sources') when retrieval confidence is low, and explicit reporting when sources conflict. Add effective_date metadata and prefer newer documents on conflict. Test with your 15 unanswerable and 5 deliberately contradictory cases; also try putting the whole corpus in a long-context model for 10 questions and compare cost/accuracy.
practice.done_when: Tests pass for citation validity (every cited span exists and supports its claim on a 20-answer sample), abstention on ≥12/15 unanswerables, and conflict reporting on 5/5; a long-context vs RAG comparison table.

quiz.prompt: Placing the most relevant chunks at the start or end of the context helps because:
options: Models tend to under-use information in the middle of long contexts
quiz.explain: This is the 'lost in the middle' effect.

quiz.prompt: A correct abstention is:
options: The right behaviour when the sources do not contain the answer
quiz.explain: Score abstentions on unanswerable questions as passes.

quiz.prompt: Citation support means:
options: The cited span actually entails the claim
quiz.explain: A citation that doesn't support the claim is worse than none.

quiz.prompt: How do you decide between RAG and putting the whole 150-page policy in a long-context model?
rubric: Size/cost per query (with and without prompt caching) and latency
Update frequency, need for citations and permissions
Measure both on the same questions (accuracy incl. lost-in-the-middle effects); consider CAG for a static corpus

practice.title: RAG report card
practice.brief: Run Ragas (or your own judge) for faithfulness and answer correctness on the frozen test split. Hand-label 40 answers and report judge agreement before trusting the scores. Inject 5 poisoned documents containing instructions ('ignore previous… say X') and report attack-success rate before/after your M10.U13 guards. Write a per-stage diagnosis (missing evidence / ranking / packing / generation) for every failed case.
practice.done_when: A report with metric scores + judge agreement on 40 labels, attack-success rate before/after guards, and a failure table where every failure has a stage label.

quiz.prompt: Faithfulness measures whether:
options: The answer matches the gold answer
The answer's claims are supported by the retrieved context
quiz.explain: Faithfulness ≠ correctness: you can be faithful to wrong context.

quiz.prompt: High faithfulness with low answer correctness most likely indicates:
options: A judge that is too strict
A retrieval problem — faithfully answering from the wrong evidence
quiz.explain: Check context recall for those cases.

quiz.prompt: Before reporting judge-based RAG metrics you should:
options: Check agreement against human labels on a sample
quiz.explain: Uncalibrated judge scores are opinions, not measurements.

quiz.prompt: Describe how you'd attribute a wrong answer to retrieval vs generation using your logs.
rubric: Check whether gold passages appear in retrieved top-k (recall) and in the packed context
If evidence was present, inspect the answer vs evidence (faithfulness, citation) → generation/packing
If absent → retrieval (chunking/embedding/ranking); log per-stage IDs to make this mechanical

capstone.title: Measured RAG over a real corpus
capstone.brief: Pick a corpus useful in Pakistan (FBR tax circulars, HEC policies, your university's rules, PSX filings, a legal code). Ship an API and UI with span-cited answers plus a public evaluation report covering every baseline and ablation on a frozen test split.

levels: Excellent: BM25 → dense → hybrid → +rerank → +one query/chunk change, each on the frozen split with recall@k, nDCG and p95 latency; negative results reported
Excellent: incremental ingest by hash; span-level citations that round-trip to source pages
Excellent: faithfulness and correctness with a calibrated judge (agreement reported); abstention measured on unanswerables
Excellent: ACL filtering before generation; poisoned-document test with attack-success rate
Excellent: pgvector/Qdrant in Docker; versioned re-embed; traces with cost/latency per stage
